Two-dimensional mid-domain null model of species richness

geo_mde.Rd

geo_mde() asks whether a map of species richness could arise from the shape of the land alone. In a bounded domain (an island, a country, a mountain range), ranges placed at random overlap most in the interior, so richness peaks there with no environmental cause: the mid-domain effect in two dimensions (Colwell and Lees 2000; Jetz and Rahbek 2001).

Each species keeps its observed range size (in grid cells) and its range is placed at random in the domain nsim times with the spreading-dye algorithm: a random seed cell, then growth into randomly chosen neighbouring cells, so ranges stay contiguous and follow the real coastline. Unlike RangeModel and rangemodelR, which work along one dimension or on regular grids, the domain here is any polygon, on an equal-area grid.

Ranges are built from occurrence points: range = "hull" (default) takes the cells inside the convex hull of each species' records within the domain, a common proxy for the extent of occurrence; range = "cells" uses the occupied cells only.

Usage

geo_mde(
  data,
  domain,
  res,
  species = species,
  range = c("hull", "buffer", "cells"),
  buffer = NULL,
  nsim = 199,
  conf = 0.95,
  lon = lon,
  lat = lat
)

Arguments

data

Occurrence records: an sf object of points, or a data frame with longitude and latitude columns.

domain

An sf polygon (or multipolygon) of the bounded domain.

res

Grid cell size in metres.

species

Column with species names.

range

How each species' range is built from its records: "hull" (the convex hull), "buffer" (all cells within buffer metres of a record) or "cells" (occupied cells only). Hulls suit continuous ranges on land; buffers suit species tied to patchy habitat such as reefs, coasts or mountain tops, where a hull would span unsuitable ground between distant records.

buffer

Buffer distance in metres for range = "buffer"; by default twice the cell size.

nsim

Number of randomisations.

conf

Width of the simulation interval.

lon, lat

Coordinate columns when data is not sf.

Value

A SpatRaster with layers observed (richness of the observed ranges), expected (mean of the null model), sd, lower, upper (simulation interval) and ses (standardised effect size, (observed - expected) / sd: positive where there are more species than geometry predicts). Attribute fit holds n_species, n_cells, r2 (variance in observed richness explained by the null model) and truncated (ranges that could not grow to full size because the piece of domain they started in was too small).

References

Colwell, R. K. and Lees, D. C. (2000). The mid-domain effect: geometric constraints on the geography of species richness. Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 15, 70-76. doi:10.1016/S0169-5347(99)01767-X

Jetz, W. and Rahbek, C. (2001). Geometric constraints explain much of the species richness pattern in African birds. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 98, 5661-5666. doi:10.1073/pnas.091100998

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)) {
  lux <- sf::st_read(system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra"), quiet = TRUE)
  set.seed(1)
  pts <- sf::st_sample(sf::st_union(lux), 300)
  occ <- sf::st_sf(species = sample(paste0("sp", 1:20), 300, TRUE), geometry = pts)
  m <- geo_mde(occ, lux, res = 5000, nsim = 49)
  attr(m, "fit")
}
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   n_species n_cells    r2 truncated
#>       <int>   <int> <dbl>     <int>
#> 1        20     100 0.656         0
# }
